paras: The execution of Robert Watkins and John Salter was the legal hanging of two Black men at Evergreen, Alabama, on August 6, 1915, for the murder of a white woman, Mrs. Mary Lassiter. Militia stood guard at the gallows, and wire reports said a crowd of citizens had demanded that the two men be burned. The case reached the national press as one of nine hangings of Black men in the South in a single day, a roundup the Chicago Defender reprinted under the headline "Nine Human Beings Hanged in South Within 24 Hours."

According to the Montgomery Advertiser's Evergreen correspondent, the crime was the killing of "Martha Lassiter" some twelve miles north of the town on the night of June 23. An Associated Press dispatch added that the men had also left Wiley House, a planter, for dead and burned the farmhouse, details no other report gives. The Advertiser said Watkins and Salter were arrested the next day, confessed, and were convicted at a special term of Circuit court two weeks later. Governor Henderson refused reprieves in all four Alabama cases set for that day.

Two companies of militia, or in other accounts a squad, stood guard while the men were hanged. A Memphis dispatch said the soldiers were there "to prevent disorder, threatened by citizens who wanted the blacks burned," and the New-York Tribune's version said "a crowd yelled and screamed to have the negroes burned." No report describes any move on the prisoners.

Sheriff Williams carried out the hanging shortly after 11 o'clock, with Watkins going first and dying in eight minutes and Salter dying almost at once. More than two thousand people came to town, the Advertiser reported, but only a few were allowed to watch, and its account mentions neither the militia nor any crowd threat.

White coverage came in three strands. The Advertiser's local special, headlined "Two Negroes Hanged for Lassiter Murder," stressed the men's confession and the smiles with which they mounted the scaffold. The AP dispatch from Montgomery, carried in Americus, Washington, Hattiesburg, Pine Bluff and Pensacola on August 6 and 7, reported Evergreen as one of four hangings in which men were "legally executed" in the state that day. A Memphis roundup, in Milwaukee, South Bend, New York, Alexandria and Washington and later in weekly ready-print, set the case beside two lynchings in Oklahoma and Florida under headlines such as "Law and Lynchers Take Nine Lives."
Several versions garbled the case, placing the murder "at Cullman," the site of a separate hanging of a white man, or counting "three negroes" hanged at Evergreen.

The Chicago Defender printed the Memphis roundup on its front page on August 14 as a special, calling the dead "Afro-Americans" and adding a deck that said only four of the nine hangings were, "it is alleged," legal, while five were "Cold Blooded Murders." Its text said the militia had prevented a mob "from burning the dead bodies," where the white versions said the mob wanted to burn the men. The Denver Star reprinted the Defender's text, with credit, on August 21.

The murdered woman is "Mrs. Mary Lassiter" in most dispatches, "Lasseter" in some, and "Martha Lassiter" in the local Advertiser account. The crowd's demand for burning appears only in the Memphis roundup and the Tribune, while the Advertiser's Evergreen report is silent on it.

reader.title: Execution of Robert Watkins and John Salter
bases: Watkins and Salter were hanged by the sheriff after conviction (A1, A4), while a crowd that wanted them burned was held back by militia (A5, A7); the violence the papers report beyond the legal execution is a threat.

The two men died by legal hanging carried out by Sheriff Williams after conviction at a special term of Circuit court (A4), described as legal executions by every report (A1, A2, A16); the crowd that wanted them burned killed no one (A5, A7).

The Advertiser's own Evergreen special (A4), the AP Montgomery dispatch (A1, A2) and the Memphis roundup (A5, A6, A16) agree on the hanging of the two men; the crowd's demand for burning rests on the Memphis roundup and the Tribune's telegraph (A5, A7) and is absent, not denied, in A4.

accounts.gist: A routine execution: the men confessed, were tried at a special term, died calmly, and few of the 2,000 visitors were admitted; no crowd threat is mentioned.

framing.detail: The Advertiser headlined 'Two Negroes Hanged for Lassiter Murder' and dwelt on their confession and 'remarkable nerve'.
AP and Memphis roundups folded Evergreen into 'Four Hang in Alabama' and 'Law and Lynchers Take Nine Lives', treating the crowd's demand as a one-line detail.
The Defender ran the roundup as 'Nine Human Beings Hanged in South Within 24 Hours', with a deck saying five of the nine were 'Cold Blooded Murders'; the Denver Star reprinted it.
